docs/OnixRuntime.Api.Rendering.GameBlock.summary: Class GameBlockRenderer Namespace OnixRuntime.Api.Rendering Assembly OnixRuntime.dll Allows you to render game blocks, this is a little more involved of a process than calling a magical render block function, but the results are pretty good. You get almost every block and their hardcoded behavior handled for you, occlusion if you set it up. It's still a lot less involved than implementing all of this yourself! public class GameBlockRenderer : MemoryAddressContainer Inheritance object MemoryAddressContainer GameBlockRenderer Inherited Members MemoryAddressContainer.SetMemoryAddress(nint) MemoryAddressContainer.Equals(object) MemoryAddressContainer.GetHashCode() object.Equals(object, object) object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Properties Cache This is what the GameBlockRenderer goes to everytime it needs a block. This lets you cheat by changing the cache yourself to manipulate the rendering. Very notably, UseOccluder needs to be properly setup in order to work. The cache contains a region of 20x20x20 blocks, which is meant to be a subchunk and two blocks around it. Going outside the cache usually will lead to air being returned. public GameBlockRendererCache Cache { get; } Property Value GameBlockRendererCache CurrentBlock You should probably use SetupRenderingForBlock(BlockPos, Block, BlockLightingType) instead of setting this yourself. The block for the shape, set it to the block you're about to render public Block? CurrentBlock { get; set; } Property Value Block CurrentPosition You should probably use SetupRenderingForBlock(BlockPos, Block, BlockLightingType) instead of setting this yourself. The position of the block in the world. public BlockPos CurrentPosition { get; set; } Property Value BlockPos CurrentScale You should probably leave this alone at all times, this messes up a lot of stuff. Can be quite funny to mess with it though. SetupRenderingForBlock(BlockPos, Block, BlockLightingType) does set that to 1.0f for you. If you DO want to scale, you should use PostScaleOffset because this one does not do good scaling with many blocks. public float CurrentScale { get; set; } Property Value float CurrentShapeSet You should probably use SetupRenderingForBlock(BlockPos, Block, BlockLightingType) instead of setting this yourself. Tells the renderer if the CurrentVisualShape is set or not. Best to leave this at false. public bool CurrentShapeSet { get; set; } Property Value bool CurrentVisualShape You should probably use SetupRenderingForBlock(BlockPos, Block, BlockLightingType) instead of setting this yourself. The current visual shape of the block being rendered. You should just set CurrentBlock and CurrentPosition then explicitly set CurrentShapeSet to false. This will make the game retrieve the proper shape on its own, which will likely be better than what you will come up with. You can even collect it after it is done rendering the block too! public BoundingBox CurrentVisualShape { get; set; } Property Value BoundingBox IsRenderingExtra This is to tell the renderer that it is rendering the extra block, or the block at the layer 1. This is for waterlogged blocks or foliage with snow in it. You would use GetExtraBlock(BlockPos) to get the extra block, you'd SetupRenderingForBlock(BlockPos, Block, BlockLightingType) and after that, set this to true. Remember to not render it if it's air. public bool IsRenderingExtra { get; set; } Property Value bool IsRenderingGui This tells the renderer that you are rendering it in the UI. It does some special things, like disabling lighting, culling, ambient occlusion, etc. public bool IsRenderingGui { get; set; } Property Value bool LightingType The type of lighting to use when rendering blocks. You can have it flat, with ambient occlusion or just normals. public GameBlockRenderer.BlockLightingType LightingType { get; set; } Property Value GameBlockRenderer.BlockLightingType Region The WorldBlocks this game block renderer uses. You should probably not use this in most cases unless it's the only one you got access to. public WorldBlocks Region { get; } Property Value WorldBlocks RenderingLayer This is to tell the renderer which block layer it's rendering right now. You can set it to the RawRenderLayer and forget it. You should not rely on the specific values as they changed over the versions. public int RenderingLayer { get; set; } Property Value int UseNormals If it should use the normals vertex attribute. Do see LightingType as the usefulness of normals depends on the lighting type. You should set this to false in most cases. public bool UseNormals { get; set; } Property Value bool UseOccluder The occluder is what allows the faces that aren't visible to not be rendered. This does not do camera based culling, only at the face level, seeing if a block is hiding that face. This is very useful but requires a little more work to work properly. You need to make sure the Cache is properly filled up/reset with a position that can be accessed in the cache. The cache contains a region of 20x20x20 blocks, which is meant to be a subchunk and two blocks around it. Going outside the cache usually will lead to air being returned and no culling/occlusion. public bool UseOccluder { get; set; } Property Value bool Methods GetTexture(BlockPos, Block, BlockFace, int) Returns the coordinates for this face on the TerrainAtlas. This function needs no setup to properly work. public TextureUVCoordinates GetTexture(BlockPos renderPosition, Block blockToRender, BlockFace blockFace, int forcedVariant = -1) Parameters renderPosition BlockPos This will be where the block will be rendered but the world block doesn't have to match the blockToRender. The issue is that if you do UseOccluder, this will use the Cache to determine if it should be occluded or not. Now if the block you're trying to do isn't actually in the world, but you still want to occlude, you could manually fill up the cache. blockToRender Block The block you want to render. blockFace BlockFace The face of the block you're trying to render. Just remember, not everything is a full block and this won't give the best result on non-full blocks. forcedVariant int This is to force a specific variant of a block, you should probably not touch that, the game half hardcodes values for those. Returns TextureUVCoordinates The face's UV in the atlas. RenderBlock(GameMeshBuilder, BlockPos, Block) If you're looking for opacity or tinting, look at RenderBlockTinted(GameMeshBuilder, BlockPos, Block, ColorF). This function does require setup before it is used. You can get SetupRenderingForBlock(BlockPos, Block, BlockLightingType) to do most of it for you. You should try to batch blocks into a single mesh whenever possible. You should re-use that mesh as generating those meshes can be quite slow. You will probably want to SetMaterialCustom(string, bool) use a custom material like "terrain_alpha" or "terrain_blend" or "terrain_opaque" (note that "terrain_blend" decided to not work on 1.21.40 specifically...) Now to use this, you will need a GameMeshBuilder that has a session started. Remember that this function can only render with Quad. For testing, you should likely use applyReverseOriginOffsetIf3D and add -32 or something to the height of PostTransformOffset. This will let you see the results so you know you're doing something right. Once you're ready to get serious, you can put it to false and offset it by the invert of the first block on the x and y (assuming you're rendering a group of blocks of course.) This will then let you offset it where you want without much precision loss using PushTransformation(TransformationMatrix, bool) before rendering the mesh. Once you rendered every block you want, call Build(bool, bool) to get the mesh out of it. Note: You should never render an air block. You'll get the update block otherwise. Don't hesitate to ask for help if you do need some. You can also look at the examples below. public void RenderBlock(GameMeshBuilder meshBuilder, BlockPos renderPosition, Block blockToRender) Parameters meshBuilder GameMeshBuilder A GameMeshBuilder That has started. renderPosition BlockPos The position at which you want to render that block, this will render it at that position in the world, but also take things like rotation for that position. (How a few blocks like grass or sand rotates depending on its world position.) It doesn't have to match where the block actually is or actually exist in the world. Note that if you DO use UseOccluder you will absolutely want to trick the Cache if the position does not match to ensure the desired result. blockToRender Block The block that you actually do want to render. Examples This example shows how to render a block at a specific position. Specifically, mirror a block that's in the world. Taking the player's targeted block and rendering it two blocks above. private void OnWorldRender(RendererWorld gfx, float delta) { // Check if we are even looking at a block. if (Onix.LocalPlayer is { Raycast: { Type: RaycastResultType.Block } }) { // Get the block we're targeting's position in the world. BlockPos blockPos = Onix.LocalPlayer.Raycast.BlockPosition; // Get is as a block. Block block = Onix.Region!.GetBlock(blockPos); // This lets us support waterlogging / snow with foliage inside. Block extraBlock = Onix.Region!.GetExtraBlock(blockPos); // Get the coordinates of the second block from the one we're targeting. BlockPos desiredRenderPosition = blockPos.Up.Up; // Never render an air block guys! if (!block.IsAir()) { // Start a new mesh builder session with quads. using (var session = gfx.NewMeshBuilderSession(MeshBuilderPrimitiveType.Quad, ColorF.White, TexturePath.TerrainAtlas)) { // Usually for more complex movement, you'd probably want to use a transformation matrix, especially that you would have saved the mesh. // For now, this will offset the vertices further, causing them to be where we want them. // And since we're rendering a block that is actually in the world, it means we won't have to mess with the cache. session.Builder.PostTransformOffset = session.Builder.PostTransformOffset + new Vec3(desiredRenderPosition - blockPos); // Get our wonderful block renderer. var blockRenderer = gfx.BlockRenderer; // Let it do the basic configuring for us, no need to go into the weeds here. blockRenderer.SetupRenderingForBlock(blockPos, block); // We don't want to hide any faces in this case, plus setting up the occluder is a bit more efforts. // Since we're not using an occluder, no real need to reset the cache. blockRenderer.UseOccluder = false; // If we want biome tinting to work, we have to reset the cache. You may not care about that so that's why it's manual. blockRenderer.ResetBiomeCache(blockPos); // Add the block onto our mesh builder session. // For one block it's fine to not use an occluder but for larger volumes, you should consider setting it up. blockRenderer.RenderBlock(session.Builder, blockPos, block); // Render the second layer if any. Remember, don't render air. Don't do it guys. if (!extraBlock.IsAir()) { // Setup this new block at our new position. blockRenderer.SetupRenderingForBlock(blockPos, extraBlock); // We're rendering an extra block right now, not the main block. Let it know. blockRenderer.IsRenderingExtra = true; // And render that one too! blockRenderer.RenderBlock(session.Builder, blockPos, extraBlock); } // For lighting, it usually puts UVs from the light texture into the UV1 slot of the vertices. // Since we can't provide it, we make sure it's not rendering from whatever was last bound there. session.Builder.DisableUv1(); } // Now, if we had anything to render, when that } calls Dispose() it should render our block with the material we picked. } } } This example shows how to render a single block that is not actually in the world at a specific position. private void OnWorldRender(RendererWorld gfx, float delta) { // Easy example: Render a specific block that is not really in the world. // Gets the water and fence block we want to render. (the ?? is because the fence changed its name at some point, so this handles both cases) Block oakFenceBlock = (Onix.World!.BlockRegistry.GetBlock("oak_fence", 0) ?? Onix.World.BlockRegistry.GetBlock("fence"))!; Block extraBlockWater = Onix.World.BlockRegistry.GetBlock("water")!; // Get the coordinates of where we want to render, in my case it'll be at 5, 5, 5. BlockPos fakeBlockRenderPosition = BlockPos.FromString("5 5 5"); // Start a new mesh builder session with quads. using (var session = gfx.NewMeshBuilderSession(MeshBuilderPrimitiveType.Quad, ColorF.White, TexturePath.TerrainAtlas)) { // Get our wonderful block renderer. var blockRenderer = gfx.BlockRenderer; // We'll need to cheat the cache to get the result we want, first we have to reset it. // In this case, we could probably get away with not resetting it, but because of the water // We have to reset it and lie, otherwise it becomes a flat plane. blockRenderer.ResetCache(fakeBlockRenderPosition); // If we want biome tinting to work, we have to reset the cache. You may not care about that so that's why it's manual. blockRenderer.ResetBiomeCache(fakeBlockRenderPosition); // This is our actual block we want to render, we'll put it in the cache for good measure blockRenderer.Cache.SetBlock(fakeBlockRenderPosition, oakFenceBlock); // I also want this fence to be waterlogged, so let's set that too. blockRenderer.Cache.SetExtraBlock(fakeBlockRenderPosition, extraBlockWater); // Let it do the basic configuring for us, no need to go into the weeds here. // We give it the position we tampered with in the cache. blockRenderer.SetupRenderingForBlock(fakeBlockRenderPosition, oakFenceBlock); // We don't want to hide any faces in this case, plus setting up the occluder is a bit more efforts. blockRenderer.UseOccluder = false; // Add the block onto our mesh builder session. // For one block it's fine to not use an occluder but for larger volumes, you should consider setting it up. blockRenderer.RenderBlock(session.Builder, fakeBlockRenderPosition, oakFenceBlock); // Render the second layer, in this case we know we have one so no checks. // Setup this new block at our new position. blockRenderer.SetupRenderingForBlock(fakeBlockRenderPosition, extraBlockWater); // We're rendering an extra block right now, not the main block. Let it know. blockRenderer.IsRenderingExtra = true; // And render that one too! blockRenderer.RenderBlock(session.Builder, fakeBlockRenderPosition, extraBlockWater); // For lighting, it usually puts UVs from the light texture into the UV1 slot of the vertices. // Since we can't provide it, we make sure it's not rendering from whatever was last bound there. session.Builder.DisableUv1(); } // Now, if we had anything to render, when that } calls Dispose() it should render our block with the material we picked. } This example shows how to render more than one block, in this case part of a chunk. You can adapt it or learn from it to build your own larger meshes but it should be a good starting point. private GameMesh? _subChunkMesh = null; private void OnWorldRender(RendererWorld gfx, float delta) { // Only generate a mesh when we don't have one already. if (_subChunkMesh is null) { var mb = gfx.MeshBuilder; var blockRenderer = gfx.BlockRenderer; // We start our new session here, note that I'm not applying the reverse origin, since we're going to render it at the origin. // Well at least at the mesh level. mb.New(ColorF.White, MeshBuilderPrimitiveType.Quad, false); // Get our coordinates for what we want to pick up. // We'll take two sub chunks from height 0. We'll pick the chunkToGrab chunk data. // Of course, you can do less or more, you have to split it up for the cache though. int subChunksToInclude = 2; ChunkPos chunkToGrab = new(0, 0); BlockPos chunkStartPos = new(chunkToGrab.X * 16, 0, chunkToGrab.Y * 16); // We're going to offset our first block to be at 0,0, 0 when the mesh is built, which is the invert of our first block's position. mb.PostTransformOffset = new Vec3(-chunkStartPos); for (int currentSubChunk = 0; currentSubChunk < subChunksToInclude; currentSubChunk++) { // Reset our cache to this subchunk. I'll also surround with air so the sides are visible. // The bottom and top will also be surrounded, but not of every subchunk, only the first and last. bool shouldSurroundTopAndBottom = currentSubChunk == 0 || currentSubChunk == (subChunksToInclude - 1); blockRenderer.ResetCacheAndSurroundInAir(chunkStartPos.WithY(chunkStartPos.Y + currentSubChunk * 16), true, shouldSurroundTopAndBottom); // If we want biome tinting to work, we have to reset the cache. You may not care about that so that's why it's manual. blockRenderer.ResetBiomeCache(chunkStartPos.WithY(chunkStartPos.Y + currentSubChunk * 16)); for (int x = 0; x < 16; x++) { for (int y = 0; y < 16; y++) { for (int z = 0; z < 16; z++) { // This gets our coordinates from our for loops into a BlockPos BlockPos currentBlockPos = new(chunkStartPos.X + x, chunkStartPos.Y + y + currentSubChunk * 16, chunkStartPos.Z + z); Block blockAtPos = Onix.Region!.GetBlock(currentBlockPos); // Don't render air guys! if (blockAtPos.IsAir()) continue; // Setup our block as before, no need for anything fancy. blockRenderer.SetupRenderingForBlock(currentBlockPos, blockAtPos); // Tell it to occlude faces we can't see, this doesn't do anything with the camera, just at the mesh level. // Still, that's very good and since we've set up the cache, it should be able to detect what it needs. blockRenderer.UseOccluder = true; // And send it! blockRenderer.RenderBlock(mb, currentBlockPos, blockAtPos); // And now, to support the second layer, waterlogging, etc. Block extraBlockAtPos = Onix.Region!.GetExtraBlock(currentBlockPos); if (!extraBlockAtPos.IsAir()) { // Just don't render air! // Set that block up. blockRenderer.SetupRenderingForBlock(currentBlockPos, extraBlockAtPos); // We're rendering an extra block right now, not the main block. Let it know. blockRenderer.IsRenderingExtra = true; // Send that one too, great that one block is done and added to our mesh. blockRenderer.RenderBlock(mb, currentBlockPos, extraBlockAtPos); } } } } } // For lighting, it usually puts UVs from the light texture into the UV1 slot of the vertices. // Since we can't provide it, we make sure it's not rendering from whatever was last bound there. // This has to be done before we build/render the mesh. session.Builder.DisableUv1(); // Okay, we've just finished adding all those blocks, that probably took some time but now time to convert it to a mesh. // That way, we don't have to do all that work again. Make sure to put immediate to false. _subChunkMesh = mb.Build(false); } if (_subChunkMesh is not null) { // Now, to render it. It's quite tricky to find a material, but this seems to give decent results. // Pretty well with almost every block, doesn't support blending or tinted glass very well though. // This is why we have render layers exposed now, so you can try to do different things, good luck. gfx.SetMaterialParameters(new GameMaterialParameters() { AlphaTest = true, Uv = true, Gradient = true, }); // Now we have to position it, remembered how we made sure to render it at 0,0,0? // Now we have to move it not only back into view but where we actually want to render it. // Whatever position we do give, will represent the block in the bottom corner with the smallest coordinates. // I'll render mine at 16, 10, 16. You can pick any coordinates in 3d, sub-coordinates. Rotate it, scale it, have fun! TransformationMatrix transformation = TransformationMatrix.TranslateWorldPosition(16, 10, 16); using (_ = gfx.PushTransformation(transformation)) { // Finally, while that transformation is applied, let's render our mesh. // Don't forget to give it the terrain texture atlas! // And that's done, you should see a copy of your chunk where you rendered it. // The inside should be hollow if you set up your cache and enabled UseOccluder. // To reflect the changes of course, you'd have to rebuild the mesh. gfx.RenderMesh(_subChunkMesh, ColorF.White, TexturePath.TerrainAtlas); } } } RenderBlockTinted(GameMeshBuilder, BlockPos, Block, ColorF) Sorry, I don't really want to put every example here again, please see RenderBlock(GameMeshBuilder, BlockPos, Block) for examples. This function does require setup before it is used. You can get SetupRenderingForBlock(BlockPos, Block, BlockLightingType) to do most of it for you. You should try to batch blocks into a single mesh whenever possible. You should re-use that mesh as generating those meshes can be quite slow. You will probably want to SetMaterialCustom(string, bool) use a custom material like "terrain_alpha" or "terrain_blend" or "terrain_opaque" (note that "terrain_blend" decided to not work on 1.21.40 specifically...) Now to use this, you will need a GameMeshBuilder that has a session started. Remember that this function can only render with Quad. For testing, you should likely use applyReverseOriginOffsetIf3D and add -32 or something to the height of PostTransformOffset. This will let you see the results so you know you're doing something right. Once you're ready to get serious, you can put it to false and offset it by the invert of the first block on the x and y (assuming you're rendering a group of blocks of course.) This will then let you offset it where you want without much precision loss using PushTransformation(TransformationMatrix, bool) before rendering the mesh. Once you rendered every block you want, call Build(bool, bool) to get the mesh out of it. Note: You should never render an air block. You'll get the update block otherwise. Don't hesitate to ask for help if you do need some. You can also look at the examples in RenderBlock(GameMeshBuilder, BlockPos, Block). public void RenderBlockTinted(GameMeshBuilder meshBuilder, BlockPos renderPosition, Block blockToRender, ColorF tint) Parameters meshBuilder GameMeshBuilder A GameMeshBuilder That has started. renderPosition BlockPos The position at which you want to render that block, this will render it at that position in the world, but also take things like rotation for that position. (How a few blocks like grass or sand rotates depending on its world position.) It doesn't have to match where the block actually is or actually exist in the world. Note that if you DO use UseOccluder you will absolutely want to trick the Cache if the position does not match to ensure the desired result. blockToRender Block The block that you actually do want to render. tint ColorF The tint to use when rendering. Note that for opacity, you'd give a white color with the desired opacity. ResetBiomeCache(BlockPos) This resets the biome cache for this subchunk, you should call if you want biome tinting to apply. This is obviously made to render subchunks, but if you're just rendering a single block, you can just give it that position as is. public void ResetBiomeCache(BlockPos worldSubChunkStartPosition) Parameters worldSubChunkStartPosition BlockPos The starting position of your sub chunk. ResetCache(BlockPos) This resets the cache to an empty state, you should call this before doing anything with the cache. This will do -2 to the position you add to it, so you should just give it the start of your subchunk. This is obviously made to render subchunks, but if you're just rendering a single block, you can just give it that position as is. When rendering a subchunk, if you want the sides to render too, you should call ResetCacheAndSurroundInAir(BlockPos, bool, bool) instead to surround it in air at the same time. public void ResetCache(BlockPos worldSubChunkStartPosition) Parameters worldSubChunkStartPosition BlockPos The starting position of your sub chunk. ResetCacheAndSurroundInAir(BlockPos, bool, bool) This resets the cache to an empty state, you should call this before doing anything with the cache. This will do -2 to the position you add to it, so you should just give it the start of your subchunk. This is obviously made to render subchunks, but if you're just rendering a single block, you can just give it that position as is. When rendering a subchunk, if you want the sides to render too, this is the function for it! public void ResetCacheAndSurroundInAir(BlockPos worldSubChunkStartPosition, bool sides = true, bool topAndBottom = true) Parameters worldSubChunkStartPosition BlockPos The starting position of your sub chunk. sides bool True if you want the sides to be surrounded by air. topAndBottom bool True if you want the top and bottom faces to be surrounded SetupRenderingForBlock(BlockPos, Block, BlockLightingType) Sets up a lot of renderer parameters for you. Note that you should make your changes after calling this function if the defaults don't satisfy you. Note that this does not touch UseOccluder. You are responsible for managing this bit yourself as it requires more flexibility than this simple function can provide. public void SetupRenderingForBlock(BlockPos pos, Block block, GameBlockRenderer.BlockLightingType lightingType = BlockLightingType.BakedWithAmbientOcclusion) Parameters pos BlockPos The position of the block in the world. block Block The block to set it up for. lightingType GameBlockRenderer.BlockLightingType The kind of lighting you want. Remarks Here is what this function does for you. CurrentShapeSet = false; CurrentBlock = block; CurrentPosition = pos; RenderingLayer = block.RawRenderLayer; IsRenderingExtra = false; IsRenderingGui = false; UseNormals = false; LightingType = lightingType; CurrentScale = 1.0f;

docs/OnixRuntime.Api.Rendering.GameBlock.summary: Class GameBlockRendererCache Namespace OnixRuntime.Api.Rendering Assembly OnixRuntime.dll IMPORTANT: You HAVE to Reset(BlockPos) the cache if you plan on making use of it, getting or setting any values out of it. This is what the GameBlockRenderer goes to everytime it needs a block. This lets you cheat by changing the cache yourself to manipulate the rendering. Very notably, UseOccluder needs to be properly setup in order to work. Now this cache has a 20x20x20 area. You don't want to be rendering blocks outside of that. This cache is meant to contain a subchunk and two blocks outwards. You reset it with the starting position of your subchunk (+15 x,y,z should be the last/end position of the subchunk). Often, you will want the edges of your chunks to not be culled, so you can call SurroundInAir(bool, bool, bool) after resetting it to make it believe the edges are air. public class GameBlockRendererCache : MemoryAddressContainer Inheritance object MemoryAddressContainer GameBlockRendererCache Inherited Members MemoryAddressContainer.SetMemoryAddress(nint) MemoryAddressContainer.Equals(object) MemoryAddressContainer.GetHashCode() object.Equals(object, object) object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Methods GetBlock(BlockPos) Warning: This does not go to the outside world when the value is not in the cache. Warning: Make sure the cache has been reset with a logical position for what you're trying to do before using this function. You should probably not use this function. You will get whatever is in the cache. In the case of blocks, they are reset to an update block. Out of range will always be air even when the game is doing it. public Block GetBlock(BlockPos worldPos) Parameters worldPos BlockPos The position in the world to get from the cache. Returns Block Whatever block is cached at that position or air if out of range. GetBlockGraphics(BlockPos) Warning: This does not go to the outside world when the value is not in the cache. Warning: Make sure the cache has been reset with a logical position for what you're trying to do before using this function. You should probably not use this function. Retrieves the BlockGraphics currently cached at the given position. Out of range will return the default "air" graphics. public BlockGraphics GetBlockGraphics(BlockPos worldPos) Parameters worldPos BlockPos The position in the world to get from the cache. Returns BlockGraphics The cached BlockGraphics at the specified position, or air graphics if out of range. GetBrightness(BlockPos) Warning: This does not go to the outside world when the value is not in the cache. Warning: Make sure the cache has been reset with a logical position for what you're trying to do before using this function. You should probably not use this function. You will get whatever is in the cache. In the case of lighting, it's usually 15 or the maximum light emission. public BrightnessLevels GetBrightness(BlockPos worldPos) Parameters worldPos BlockPos The position in the world to get from the cache. Returns BrightnessLevels Whatever brightness levels are cached at that position or max if out of range. GetExtraBlock(BlockPos) Warning: This does not go to the outside world when the value is not in the cache. Warning: Make sure the cache has been reset with a logical position for what you're trying to do before using this function. You should probably not use this function. You will get whatever is in the cache in the second layer (layer 1). In the case of blocks, they are reset to an update block. Out of range will always be air even when the game is doing it. This extra block is used for waterlogging or having foliage inside snow layers. public Block GetExtraBlock(BlockPos worldPos) Parameters worldPos BlockPos The position in the world to get from the cache. Returns Block Whatever block is cached at that position or air if out of range. GetExtraBlockGraphics(BlockPos) Warning: This does not go to the outside world when the value is not in the cache. Warning: Make sure the cache has been reset with a logical position for what you're trying to do before using this function. You should probably not use this function. Retrieves the BlockGraphics currently cached at the given position for the second layer (layer 1). This is used for extra blocks such as waterlogging or foliage inside snow layers. Out of range will return the default "air" graphics. public BlockGraphics GetExtraBlockGraphics(BlockPos worldPos) Parameters worldPos BlockPos The position in the world to get from the cache. Returns BlockGraphics The cached BlockGraphics for the extra block at the specified position, or air graphics if out of range. IsInCache(BlockPos, bool) Tells you if a position is included in the cache or if it's outside the bounds of the mighty cache. public bool IsInCache(BlockPos position, bool paddingOfOneBlock = true) Parameters position BlockPos The position to check for. paddingOfOneBlock bool If true, it will return false for blocks on the edge of the cache, making sure the position can be surrounded. Returns bool True when the position is included within the cache. Reset(BlockPos) This resets the cache to an empty state, you should call this before doing anything with the cache. This will do -2 to the position you add to it, so you should just give it the start of your subchunk. This is obviously made to render subchunks, but if you're just rendering a single block, you can just give it that position as is. When rendering a subchunk, if you want the sides to render too, you can call SurroundInAir(bool, bool, bool) after this to make it believe the edges are air. public void Reset(BlockPos worldSubChunkStartPosition) Parameters worldSubChunkStartPosition BlockPos The starting position of your sub chunk. SetBlock(BlockPos, Block, bool) Warning: This does not go to the outside world when the value is not in the cache. Warning: Make sure the cache has been reset with a logical position for what you're trying to do before using this function. You should probably not use this function. This function sets a block in the cache at that position if not out of bounds. This lets you manipulate culling and maybe rendering of a few blocks. public void SetBlock(BlockPos worldPos, Block block, bool setGraphics = false) Parameters worldPos BlockPos The position in the world where you want to set the value. block Block The block to make the renderer believe is present there. setGraphics bool If the BlockGraphics should be set. Usually you always want this false, the game will retrieve it if it needs it. SetBlockGraphics(BlockPos, BlockGraphics) Warning: This does not go to the outside world when the value is not in the cache. Warning: Make sure the cache has been reset with a logical position for what you're trying to do before using this function. You should probably not use this function. Sets the BlockGraphics in the cache at the given position if not out of bounds. This lets you manipulate rendering and culling visuals for blocks. public void SetBlockGraphics(BlockPos worldPos, BlockGraphics graphics) Parameters worldPos BlockPos The position in the world where the graphics should be set. graphics BlockGraphics The BlockGraphics instance to set at the specified position. SetBrightness(BlockPos, BrightnessLevels) Warning: This does not go to the outside world when the value is not in the cache. Warning: Make sure the cache has been reset with a logical position for what you're trying to do before using this function. You should probably not use this function. This will set the value of the brightness levels in the cache at that position if not out of bounds. public void SetBrightness(BlockPos worldPos, BrightnessLevels brightness) Parameters worldPos BlockPos The position in the world where you want to set the value. brightness BrightnessLevels The brightness levels you want to set at that position. SetExtraBlock(BlockPos, Block, bool) Warning: This does not go to the outside world when the value is not in the cache. Warning: Make sure the cache has been reset with a logical position for what you're trying to do before using this function. You should probably not use this function. This function sets a block in the cache at that position for the second layer (layer 1) if not out of bounds. This lets you manipulate culling and maybe rendering of a few blocks. Extra blocks are used for waterlogging or having foliage inside snow layers. public void SetExtraBlock(BlockPos worldPos, Block block, bool setGraphics = false) Parameters worldPos BlockPos The position in the world where the block should be set. block Block The block to set at the specified position. setGraphics bool A value indicating whether to update the graphics for the block. true to update the graphics; otherwise, false. SetExtraBlockGraphics(BlockPos, BlockGraphics) Warning: This does not go to the outside world when the value is not in the cache. Warning: Make sure the cache has been reset with a logical position for what you're trying to do before using this function. You should probably not use this function. Sets the BlockGraphics in the cache at the given position for the second layer (layer 1) if not out of bounds. This is used for extra blocks such as waterlogging or foliage inside snow layers. public void SetExtraBlockGraphics(BlockPos worldPos, BlockGraphics graphics) Parameters worldPos BlockPos The position in the world where the graphics should be set. graphics BlockGraphics The BlockGraphics instance to set for the extra block at the specified position. SurroundInAir(bool, bool, bool) Warning: Make sure the cache has been reset with a logical position for what you're trying to do before using this function. This surrounds the sub chunk in air, only in the cache of course, making it so that the edges of your subchunk will render properly when using UseOccluder. Complete is just if you have messed with the cache before and need a complete reset of the edges to air. I would say only use complete if you see issues at the edge of the chunks and do more than only Reset(BlockPos) and SurroundInAir(bool, bool, bool). public void SurroundInAir(bool sides = true, bool topAndBottom = true, bool complete = false) Parameters sides bool True if you want the sides to be surrounded by air. topAndBottom bool True if you want the top and bottom faces to be surrounded complete bool Whether to do a complete reset of the edges to air.

docs/OnixRuntime.Api.Rendering.GameMater.summary: Enum GameMaterialParameterType Namespace OnixRuntime.Api.Rendering Assembly OnixRuntime.dll Represents the various parameters that can be configured for a game material. This enum is used for individual parameters, when you just want to toggle something on for a bit for example. public enum GameMaterialParameterType Fields AlphaTest = 2 Enables or disables alpha testing for the material, this will discard transparent pixels of a texture. Blending = 1 Enables or disables blending for the material, with this false, the material will be always opaque. DepthLessEqual = 5 Changes the depth test to be less than or equal instead of just less than, this will allow objects to be rendered on top of each other if they are at the same depth. DisableCulling = 7 Enables or disables culling for the material, with this false, both faces of geometry will be rendered. Gradient = 9 Allows the material to specify a vertex color. InvertCulling = 8 When true, the front face of the geometry will be rendered as the back face. Light = 6 Enables or disables lighting for the material, with this false, the material will not be affected by lights in the scene. Make sure FullBright isn't enabled in the client if you're trying to see that working. Linear = 0 Enables or disables linear filtering for the material, with this false, nearest neighbor will be used. NoDepthTest = 3 Enables or disables depth testing for the material, with this false, the material will not be rendered if it is behind another object that was also depth tested. NoDepthWrite = 4 Enables or disables depth writing for the material, with this false, the material will not write to the depth buffer, allowing other objects to be rendered on top of it even when they are below. Uv = 10 Allows the material to specify UV coordinates for textures.

NoShowThreshold How long in seconds between renders should we assume that the image wasn't shown for a while. This will reset how long it's been on screen and delay its generation. public float NoShowThreshold { get; set; } Property Value float PathProvider This function is used to get a virtual TexturePath for the SVG image rendering at a specific size. The default implementation constructs a path based on the renderer's base path and file name, appending the size in the format "{width}x{height}.png". If you need a different path structure or want to use a different method to get the texture path, you can override this function. It will upload the image for that size under whatever TexturePath you return here. public Func<SvgRenderer, Vec2I, TexturePath> PathProvider { get; set; } Property Value Func<SvgRenderer, Vec2I, TexturePath> RegenerationThreshold When rendering in non-static mode, this is the minimum size difference that will trigger a regeneration of the SVG image. This is used to avoid regenerating the image too often when the size changes too slightly. /// The default value is 64x64 pixels, meaning that the image will only be regenerated if the size changes by at least 64 pixels in either dimension. This is useful to avoid unnecessary rendering when the size changes slightly, but you can adjust it to your needs. This is to avoid animations generating a ton of images when the size changes slightly. When rendering an image at the same size for a while, a new image will only be generated regardless of this treshold. public Vec2I RegenerationThreshold { get; set; } Property Value Vec2I RenderClosestSizeUntilReady This is used to determine if the SVG renderer should render the closest size available until the texture of the proper size is ready. public bool RenderClosestSizeUntilReady { get; set; } Property Value bool SizeTransformer This function transforms the size given by the user when rendering the image into the size of the actual image data. docs/OnixRuntime.Api.Rendering.html.title: Namespace OnixRuntime.Api.Rendering | Onix Plugin Documentation
docs/OnixRuntime.Api.Rendering.html.summary: Namespace OnixRuntime.Api.Rendering Classes BlockGraphics Represents various information about a block's graphics. Notably it's texture and shape. BlockGraphics.TextureItem Represents a block's texture, having both the carried and default textures. The carried textures is used for things like UI. Example: The carried grass texture is hardcoded green while the default one is grayscale. GameBlockRenderer Allows you to render game blocks, this is a little more involved of a process than calling a magical render block function, but the results are pretty good. You get almost every block and their hardcoded behavior handled for you, occlusion if you set it up. It's still a lot less involved than implementing all of this yourself! GameBlockRendererCache IMPORTANT: You HAVE to Reset(BlockPos) the cache if you plan on making use of it, getting or setting any values out of it. This is what the GameBlockRenderer goes to everytime it needs a block. This lets you cheat by changing the cache yourself to manipulate the rendering. Very notably, UseOccluder needs to be properly setup in order to work. Now this cache has a 20x20x20 area. You don't want to be rendering blocks outside of that. This cache is meant to contain a subchunk and two blocks outwards. You reset it with the starting position of your subchunk (+15 x,y,z should be the last/end position of the subchunk). Often, you will want the edges of your chunks to not be culled, so you can call SurroundInAir(bool, bool, bool) after resetting it to make it believe the edges are air. GameMesh Represents a 3D/2D mesh in the game's renderer. You can render it later on. GameMeshBuilder Provides methods to build and render meshes at runtime. GameViewport Represents the game's viewport. You can change those, they are read once per frame. OnixDebugDraw Named, time-expiring debug drawing API. Accessible from any thread. Shapes are buffered by name and auto-rendered. The names are shared for every plugin, you should never use this over proper rendering, this is for quick and dirty debug visualization. RenderContexes Provides access to various rendering contexts and utilities. RenderContexes.AuraHelpersClass Various helper functions for aura rendering. RendererCommon Provides common rendering methods for 2D and 3D drawing operations. RendererCommon2D Provides 2D rendering functionality, including clipping and render offset utilities. RendererDirect2D Provides rendering functionality for Direct2D contexts. RendererGame Provides rendering functionality for game contexts, supporting 2D and mesh-based drawing. RendererWorld Provides rendering functionality for 3D world contexts, including mesh, item, and lighting operations. TextureAtlasItem Represents a texture in an atlas. TexturePath Represents a path to a texture resource, supporting various base locations and plugin asset resolution. TextureUVCoordinates Represents UV coordinates for a texture, including its size. Structs GameMaterialParameters Represents various rendering parameters for the state. GameMeshBuilder.GameMeshBuilderSession Represents a session for building a mesh, automatically rendering on dispose. MeshBuilderVertex Represents a vertex in the GameMeshBuilder. MeshBuilderVertexColor Represents a colored vertex in the GameMeshBuilder. MeshBuilderVertexColorNormal Represents a colored vertex with a normal in the GameMeshBuilder. MeshBuilderVertexColorUv Represents a colored vertex with UV coordinates in the GameMeshBuilder. MeshBuilderVertexColorUvNormal Represents a colored vertex with UV coordinates and a normal in the GameMeshBuilder. MeshBuilderVertexNormal Represents a vertex with a normal in the GameMeshBuilder. MeshBuilderVertexUv Represents a vertex with UV coordinates in the GameMeshBuilder. MeshBuilderVertexUvNormal Represents a vertex with UV coordinates and a normal in the GameMeshBuilder. RendererCommon.OpacityPopper Helper struct for managing opacity stack with automatic pop on dispose. RendererCommon.TransformationPopper Helper struct for managing transformation stack with automatic pop on dispose. RendererCommon2D.ClippingRectanglePopper Helper struct for managing the clipping rectangle stack with automatic pop on dispose. RendererWorld.WorldUIRenderSettingsPopper Helper struct for managing world UI render settings and transformation stack with automatic pop on dispose. Interfaces IGameRenderer Provides methods for rendering game items and meshes. Enums BlockGraphics.BlockShapes The different shapes a block can have. There are always custom blocks that they added some time ago but for vanilla blocks, these are the shapes you will encounter. FontShadowType The type of the font shadow. FontType The type of the font. FontUsage What scenario is the font used for? GameBlockRenderer.BlockLightingType How the light should be rendered GameMaterialParameterType Represents the various parameters that can be configured for a game material. This enum is used for individual parameters, when you just want to toggle something on for a bit for example. MeshBuilderPrimitiveType Specifies the primitive type for mesh building. OnixRendererType Represents the type of renderer used. RendererTextureStatus Represents the status of a renderer texture. TextAlignment Specifies text alignment options for rendering text. TexturePathBase Specifies the base location for a texture path.

ScanSignature(IEnumerable<VersionedSignature>) Scans memory within a specified address range for a versioned signature pattern. This function uses a list of signatures associated with the game version in which they started working. Signatures apply from their specified version up to but not including the next newer version. docs/OnixRuntime.Api.World.BlockShapeTyp.summary: Enum BlockShapeType Namespace OnixRuntime.Api.World Assembly OnixRuntime.dll Specifies which precomputed shape a block should provide or which shape should be used when querying block geometry. Use these values when requesting different block shape types for rendering, physics, or camera collision checks. public enum BlockShapeType Fields CameraCollision = 2 The camera collision shape. This shape is a simplified or specialized collision volume intended for camera clipping and line-of-sight calculations. It may differ from the full physical collision shape to produce smoother camera behavior. Collision = 1 The collision shape used for physical interactions. This shape represents the solid volume used by the physics system and entity movement to determine collisions and blocking. Use this when testing for movement obstruction or physical contact with the block. Outline = 0 The visual outline shape of the block. This shape is typically used for rendering selection outlines, highlighting, and any purpose where the visual silhouette of the block is required rather than its physical collision volume.

docs/OnixRuntime.Api.World.DimensionType.summary: Enum DimensionType Namespace OnixRuntime.Api.World Assembly OnixRuntime.dll Specifies the type of dimension. public enum DimensionType Fields End = 2 Nether = 1 The Nether in Minecraft is a hostile, infernal alternate dimension distinct from the Overworld and the End. It is accessible only through portals constructed from obsidian blocks, which, when ignited, shimmer with a purple, swirling energy that bridges the two realms. Upon stepping through, players are transported into a place that is immediately alien, dangerous, and richly atmospheric, designed to evoke dread, peril, and mystery. Visually, the Nether is defined by its hellish color palette—deep reds, fiery oranges, smoldering blacks, and ominous purples. The air itself seems heavy and oppressive, filled with embers drifting lazily across the screen, constantly reminding the player that this is a world of fire and decay. The terrain is largely composed of Netherrack, a porous, blood-red stone that burns eternally once set aflame, providing the Nether with its signature infernal aesthetic. Scattered among the Netherrack are dangerous hazards such as lava oceans, massive pools that stretch endlessly, glowing orange seas of molten death. Lava flows here are faster and more lethal than in the Overworld, making careful movement essential to survival. The Nether has its own distinct biomes, each contributing to its diversity of danger and atmosphere. The Nether Wastes form the baseline environment, barren and monotonous stretches of Netherrack and lava lakes populated by hostile mobs such as Zombie Piglins, Ghasts, and Magma Cubes. The Crimson Forests erupt in haunting red hues, dominated by colossal crimson fungi, twisting vines, and dense vegetation, where the air itself feels thick and hostile. Here, piglins and hoglins roam—one intelligent, bartering and aggressive, the other brutish, charging, and dangerous. In stark contrast, the Warped Forests shimmer with a haunting teal-green glow, their warped fungi and vegetation forming one of the few relatively safe havens in the Nether. Endermen stalk here, tall and menacing, their otherworldly presence emphasizing the forest’s unsettling tranquility. Then there are the Basalt Deltas, chaotic volcanic regions of jagged basalt pillars and clouds of ash particles that hang perpetually in the air, populated by magma cubes that leap and divide endlessly. Finally, Soul Sand Valleys open into vast desolate expanses of blue flame and bone blocks, their atmosphere eerily silent but frequently pierced by the echoing cries of Ghasts, creating one of the most haunting landscapes in the game. The Nether is not merely aesthetic—it is filled with structures that carry gameplay and lore significance. Nether Fortresses are vast, labyrinthine structures built from dark nether bricks, populated by wither skeletons, blazes, and hidden treasures. These fortresses are essential for progression, as they contain blaze spawners and nether wart, two crucial ingredients for brewing potions and ultimately reaching the End. More recently introduced are the Bastion Remnants, imposing strongholds of blackstone where piglins and piglin brutes guard hordes of treasure. Their broken, ruinous architecture suggests a fallen civilization, hinting at deeper lore within Minecraft’s universe. Bastions reward the brave with loot ranging from gold blocks and enchanted gear to the rare and precious Pigstep music disc and Netherite-related materials. Speaking of Netherite, the Nether is home to one of the rarest and most coveted resources in the game: Ancient Debris. Hidden deep within its crust, Ancient Debris can be smelted into Netherite scraps, which, when combined with gold, produce Netherite ingots—the material required to forge the strongest weapons and armor in the game. Mining for this resource often means braving the dangers of lava-filled caverns, explosive strip-mining, or carefully planned bed detonations, reinforcing the idea that ultimate power in Minecraft demands braving ultimate peril. The Nether also has unique mechanics that distinguish it from other dimensions. Beds explode violently when attempted to be used, dealing massive damage and setting the area ablaze. Water cannot be placed, instantly evaporating upon contact, which forces players to rethink survival strategies that are second nature in the Overworld. Movement is also affected: distances in the Nether correspond to an 8:1 scale compared to the Overworld, making Nether travel an essential mechanic for fast transportation across vast stretches of the main world. Fire is more persistent, lava flows faster, and survival requires constant awareness of surroundings. The atmosphere of the Nether is oppressive and unnerving. Its soundscape is filled with echoing growls, eerie ambient noises, and the ever-present roar of fire and lava. Ghasts scream mournfully across lava seas, and the piglins’ guttural snorts emphasize the hostile nature of the realm. The fog is tinted with ominous shades depending on the biome, reducing visibility and adding to the sense of claustrophobic danger. The Nether feels timeless, a place where no natural day-night cycle exists—only the eternal flicker of firelight and the dull glow of molten rock. Despite its hostility, the Nether is central to progression and creativity in Minecraft. It provides ingredients for potions, access to quartz for redstone contraptions, glowstone for lighting, blackstone as a cobblestone substitute, and unique flora like warped stems and crimson wood for building aesthetics. Its hostile mobs—Piglins, Blazes, Wither Skeletons, Magma Cubes, and Ghasts—each drop unique items vital for gameplay. The Nether, therefore, represents both danger and opportunity, a place of high stakes and high rewards. Philosophically and thematically, the Nether can be seen as a manifestation of chaos, destruction, and raw elemental power. It represents Minecraft's take on a "hell" dimension without overt religious symbolism: a place of eternal flame, death, and decay, but also one of hidden riches and pathways to greater challenges. Its placement as the intermediary dimension—between the tranquil, living Overworld and the void-like finality of the End—cements its role as a crucible for testing a player's survival skills, resourcefulness, and bravery. Overworld = 0 The Overworld.
